Chapter One: Discovering the Patterns That Shape Everyday Choices
Picture this: your alarm goes off in the morning. Your hand almost instinctively reaches out to hit snooze or silence it, and before you know it, your day’s begun—almost like you’re on autopilot. If you’re like most people, those first few moments are packed with tiny decisions you barely even notice. Should you get up right away? Maybe check your phone, or just stay in bed for a few extra minutes? It might not seem like much, but these little choices actually lay the foundation for your entire day. What’s wild is, most of us don’t realize just how much of what we do is shaped by old patterns—routines we set up ages ago, often without really thinking about them.
There’s one story I always come back to. It’s about someone who felt rushed, no matter how early they started their day. That sense of urgency stuck around—even on weekends. The funny thing? They didn’t notice how deeply that feeling was wired in, until a friend casually pointed out how often they checked the clock. Suddenly, the habit became visible—and with that, a little spark of curiosity lit up: what else am I doing on autopilot?
As the days went by, it became clear—routines were everywhere. From picking out breakfast, to choosing a route to work, or even how small talk started with coworkers... it all followed these invisible scripts. These scripts, shaped by things we’ve done over and over, can feel really comforting. But sometimes, they also hold us back from trying something new.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most of us don’t even notice how these patterns get started. They usually begin as small decisions, repeated until they just become part of who we are. Sometimes, we pick them up from family or early life. Maybe your parent always worried about being late—and without anyone ever saying a word, that anxious rhythm just became yours, too. Over time, these patterns turn into the lens we use to look at the world.
But here’s the thing—recognizing these habits isn’t about blaming yourself, or looking back with regret. It’s about realizing that we all carry around a collection of routines. Some we choose, and some we just absorb along the way. The first step is simply noticing them—pausing for a moment to see the choices you’re making, even in the tiniest parts of your day.
That awareness? It’s the door to change. Once you start noticing your patterns, you can decide to try something new—one small step at a time.
